    Admin Setup

    Mark Padgham

    2026-10-23

    Source: vignettes/admin-setup.Rmd
    admin-setup.Rmd

    This vignette describes how to run roreviewapi on a Digital Ocean droplet, including the editor volunteer search feature introduced in v0.2. Endpoints for that feature are described in the editor search vignette.

    It covers two cases:

    • Starting from scratch: setting up a new droplet, or a droplet that has been rebuilt.
    • General maintenance: keeping a running droplet up, up to date, and in the right hands.

    How the pieces fit together

    A few terms used throughout this vignette:

    • Droplet: a virtual server rented from Digital Ocean. It runs Linux, and you work on it by connecting from your own computer with SSH (ssh <user>@<droplet-ip>) or by using the web console button from Digital Ocean interface.
    • Docker runs programs in isolated containers. Each container is started from an image, which bundles the program with everything it needs. Docker Compose starts several containers together, as described in docker-compose.yml.
    • DNS turns a name such as reviewbot.ropensci.org into the droplet’s IP address. rOpenSci’s DNS is managed in Cloudflare, which also sits between visitors and the droplet.
    • TLS certificate: the file that lets a server prove its identity, so that connections can use HTTPS. See TLS certificate.
    • Cron runs commands on a schedule.

    docker-compose.yml defines two containers:

    • plumber is the API itself. It is built from the repository’s Dockerfile, and listens on port 8000, which is only reachable from the other container.
    • nginx answers on ports 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS), handles HTTPS with the certificate, redirects HTTP to HTTPS, and passes requests on to plumber.

    So a request travels: visitor → Cloudflare → nginx (port 443) → plumber (port 8000).

    Starting from scratch

    Follow this section to set up a new droplet. It also applies when a droplet is rebuilt: Digital Ocean’s “Rebuild” reinstalls the operating system and erases the whole disk. Everything that is not in the Git repository is then lost, in particular:

    • the .env file of secrets (see Environment variables),
    • the data directory /srv/roreviewapi/data/, which holds the database and the Gmail credential files,
    • the TLS certificate and key in /etc/ssl/cloudflare/,
    • the cron job that redeploys the service every week.

    Prerequisites

    You need:

    • SSH access to the Digital Ocean droplet, with sudo rights.
    • Access to the AirTable base containing the editor-in-chief rotation table.
    • Access to the Cloudflare account that manages the ropensci.org domain, or someone who has it.
    • Access to rOpenSci’s 1Password, where the certificate’s private key is stored.

    All commands below are run on the droplet, unless stated otherwise.

    Install Git and Docker

    Git downloads the code from GitHub. Install it with:

    sudo apt update
sudo apt install git

    Install Docker Engine and its Compose plugin by following Docker’s instructions for Ubuntu. Then check that both work:

    docker --version
docker compose version

    Docker must start automatically when the droplet boots, otherwise the service stays down after every reboot:

    sudo systemctl enable docker

    Set the Git user

    Git records a name and an email address with every commit. Set them to the bot account, for root (which runs the weekly redeploy, see Cron job) and for your own user:

    sudo git config --global user.name "ropensci-review-bot"
sudo git config --global user.email "accounts@ropensci.org"
git config --global user.name "ropensci-review-bot"
git config --global user.email "accounts@ropensci.org"

    Get the code

    The project lives in /home/shared/roreviewapi. Download it there with:

    sudo mkdir -p /home/shared
cd /home/shared
git clone https://github.com/ropensci-review-tools/roreviewapi.git
cd roreviewapi

    The remaining commands that refer to files such as .env or docker-compose.yml are run from this directory.

    Environment variables

    Secrets are not stored in the Dockerfile or anywhere else in the Git repository. They live in a .env file that exists only on the droplet. It is listed in .gitignore and .dockerignore, and is passed to the plumber container when it starts, via env_file: .env in docker-compose.yml. Because the file is not tracked by Git, git pull never overwrites it, and the values never end up in an image.

    Create .env in the project directory, with one KEY=value entry per line (no quotes and no export), and make it readable only by its owner:

    nano .env
chmod 600 .env
    Variable Description
    GITHUB_PAT GitHub personal access token (also used as GITHUB_TOKEN)
    PKGCHECK_TOKEN pkgcheck authentication token: a secret password shared by the Digital Ocean droplet and buffy
    GMAIL_SENDER Sender address used for outgoing emails
    GMAIL_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET Path to the Google OAuth client secret JSON file, e.g. /data/email/<client_secret>.json
    GMAIL_TOKEN_CACHE Path to the cached Gmail token, e.g. /data/email/gmailr_token
    GMAIL_AUTH_EMAIL Google account used to authenticate with Gmail
    AIRTABLE_API_KEY AirTable personal access token
    AIRTABLE_BASE_ID ID of the AirTable base containing the EiC rotation table
    ROREVIEWAPI_BASE_URL Public HTTPS base URL of the deployed API (https://reviewbot.ropensci.org)

    When the container starts, docker-entrypoint.sh writes these values to ~/.Renviron (setting GITHUB_TOKEN from GITHUB_PAT, and ROREV_CONTAINER=true), so that R can read them, and then starts the API.

    The two GMAIL_* file paths must be inside /data/email/. That is the container’s view of the data directory (see Data directory). Place the corresponding files in /srv/roreviewapi/data/ on the droplet.

    AirTable

    1. Generate a personal access token at https://airtable.com/create/tokens with at least the data.records:read scope on the relevant base. Set this as AIRTABLE_API_KEY.
    2. Open the AirTable base and copy the base ID from the URL (https://airtable.com/appXXXXXXXX/...). Set this as AIRTABLE_BASE_ID.

    The editor-in-chief-rotation table within that base must have period_start, period_end, and acting_eic_email fields.

    Data directory

    The data directory holds the SQLite database, the notify-email cache file, and the Gmail OAuth client secret and token cache files. It lives on the droplet, outside the containers, so that it survives when the containers are rebuilt every week. Create it with:

    sudo mkdir -p /srv/roreviewapi/data
sudo chmod 700 /srv/roreviewapi/data

    docker-compose.yml makes it available inside the plumber container as /data/email. The container must be able to write to it, because the Gmail token cache is updated during authentication.

    After a rebuild, restore its contents, and .env, from a backup (see Backing up the data and secrets). Without a backup, the database starts empty, and the Gmail authorization must be redone, following the editor search vignette.

    DNS

    The domain’s DNS is managed in Cloudflare. It needs an A record pointing the subdomain to the droplet’s IP address, for example:

    reviewbot.ropensci.org.  IN  A  <droplet-ip>

    The record must be proxied (orange cloud in the Cloudflare dashboard), not “DNS only”. The TLS certificate below is a Cloudflare Origin Certificate, which only Cloudflare trusts, so visitors must reach the droplet through Cloudflare.

    A rebuilt droplet keeps its IP address, so the record does not change. A new droplet has a new IP address, so the record must be updated.

    TLS certificate

    TLS uses a Cloudflare Origin Certificate. It secures the connection between Cloudflare and the droplet, is valid for up to 15 years, and needs no renewal on the droplet.

    1. In the Cloudflare dashboard for the domain, go to SSL/TLS → Origin Server → Create Certificate. Keep the default key type, list the hostname (reviewbot.ropensci.org), and choose a validity period.

    2. Cloudflare shows the certificate and the private key. Cloudflare does not store the private key, so it is only shown once: save it straight away. A copy of the current key is stored in rOpenSci’s 1Password. On the droplet, save them as /etc/ssl/cloudflare/origin.pem and /etc/ssl/cloudflare/origin.key.

      Create the directory and the certificate file. tee waits for input: paste the certificate, press Enter, then Ctrl+D to save:

      sudo mkdir -p /etc/ssl/cloudflare
sudo tee /etc/ssl/cloudflare/origin.pem > /dev/null

      Do the same for the private key, then make it readable only by root:

      sudo tee /etc/ssl/cloudflare/origin.key > /dev/null
sudo chmod 600 /etc/ssl/cloudflare/origin.key

      sudo tee is needed because in sudo echo ... > file the redirection runs as the current user, not as root. Sending the output to /dev/null keeps the pasted key from being printed back to the terminal.

      Check that both files are valid:

      sudo openssl x509 -in /etc/ssl/cloudflare/origin.pem -noout -subject -enddate
sudo openssl pkey -in /etc/ssl/cloudflare/origin.key -noout && echo "key OK"

      The first command shows the hostname and the expiry date. The second prints “key OK” if the key can be read.

    3. In SSL/TLS → Overview, set the encryption mode to Full (strict).

    After a rebuild, there is no need to create a new certificate. Copy the key back from 1Password, and download the certificate again from the Cloudflare dashboard (SSL/TLS → Origin Server). Save both with the tee commands above.

    Start the service

    From the project directory, build the images and start the containers in the background:

    docker compose up -d --build

    The first build takes a while. nginx only starts once plumber reports itself as healthy, which can take a few minutes.

    The compose file:

    • Mounts /srv/roreviewapi/data into the plumber container at /data/email, and sets ROREVIEWAPI_EMAIL_DB=/data/email/searches.sqlite, so that the SQLite database persists across rebuilds.
    • Reads secrets from .env via env_file.
    • Mounts /etc/ssl/cloudflare read-only into the nginx container, so that the certificate is available.
    • Sets the domain name (NGINX_SERVER_NAME), which is substituted into nginx.conf when the container starts.
    • Exposes ports 80 (HTTP → HTTPS redirect) and 443 (HTTPS).

    Cron job

    restart.sh downloads new commits and rebuilds the service (see Weekly redeploy). A cron job runs it every week. One authorized admin of the droplet needs to set it up.

    The job must run as a user that can run docker compose (either root or a member of the docker group). The following uses root’s crontab, so that the log file below can be written to /var/log.

    1. Check whether a job already exists (see Viewing, changing and checking the cron job), to avoid creating a duplicate.

    2. Open the crontab for editing. If prompted, choose an editor (nano is the easiest):

      sudo crontab -e

    3. Add the following line:

      0 0 * * 2 /bin/bash /home/shared/roreviewapi/restart.sh >> /var/log/roreviewapi-restart.log 2>&1

      This runs the script at 00:00 every Tuesday. The five leading fields are minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week (0–7, where both 0 and 7 are Sunday). crontab.guru is useful for checking a schedule. The trailing redirect appends all output, including errors, to a log file.

    4. Save and exit. Cron picks up the change automatically; no restart of the cron service is needed.

    An absolute path is required because cron does not run in the project directory. restart.sh finds the project directory (and thus .env) from its own location, so it needs no other configuration.

    Check that it works 

    docker compose ps
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://reviewbot.ropensci.org/mean

    Both containers should be running, with plumber marked healthy, and curl should print 200. Otherwise, see Troubleshooting.

    Finally, set up the uptime alert if it does not already exist.

    General maintenance

    Uptime alert

    The Software Peer Review Lead should set up a regular alert to check that the service is up. This bash script prints a message and fails if anything is wrong:

    #!/usr/bin/env bash

URL="https://reviewbot.ropensci.org"
status=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" "$URL")

if [[ "$status" != "404" ]]; then
    echo -e "reviewbot is down"
    exit 1
fi

    It should then be run regularly, for example from a ~/.bashrc file, or from a cron job.

    Weekly redeploy

    The cron job runs restart.sh every Tuesday. The script:

    1. downloads new commits with git pull --ff-only,
    2. stops the containers,
    3. deletes old images,
    4. rebuilds the images from scratch,
    5. starts the containers again.

    So changes pushed to GitHub reach the droplet within a week, and the images pick up updated R packages. The service is down while the images rebuild.

    To redeploy straight away, for example after pushing a fix, run the script by hand:

    sudo /bin/bash /home/shared/roreviewapi/restart.sh

    Viewing, changing and checking the cron job

    List the jobs in root’s crontab with:

    sudo crontab -l

    Omit sudo to list the current user’s own crontab instead. Each user has a separate crontab, so if nothing appears, check the other user (or root) that may have been used to set the job up.

    To change the job, re-open the crontab with sudo crontab -e, edit the line (for example, change the schedule fields), and save. To disable the job without deleting it, comment the line out by prefixing it with #. To remove it, delete the line. Confirm the result with sudo crontab -l.

    To check that the job ran, read the end of its log file:

    tail -n 50 /var/log/roreviewapi-restart.log

    and confirm that the containers are up with docker compose ps.

    Restarting the service

    To restart the containers without rebuilding them, for example after changing .env or installing a new certificate, run from the project directory:

    docker compose up -d --force-recreate

    To change a secret, edit .env on the droplet and restart. No change to the Dockerfile is needed.

    Backing up the data and secrets

    The data directory (/srv/roreviewapi/data/) and the .env file are the only things on the droplet that cannot be recreated from GitHub or Cloudflare. Keep a copy of them off the droplet, and refresh it before risky changes such as an operating system update, and after changing .env or redoing the Gmail authorization.

    The backup contains secrets, so store it somewhere safe, such as rOpenSci’s 1Password, rather than in email, chat or a shared drive.

    Downloading a backup

    1. On the droplet, stop the API briefly, so that the database is not being written to while it is copied:

      cd /home/shared/roreviewapi
docker compose stop plumber

    2. Pack the data directory and .env into one archive in your home directory, make it yours so that it can be downloaded, and start the API again:

      sudo tar -czf ~/roreviewapi-backup.tar.gz -C / srv/roreviewapi/data home/shared/roreviewapi/.env
sudo chown $USER ~/roreviewapi-backup.tar.gz
docker compose start plumber

      -C / makes the paths in the archive start from the root of the disk, so that they can be restored to the same places.

    3. On your own computer, download the archive with scp, which copies files over SSH. <user> and <droplet-ip> are the same as for ssh:

      scp <user>@<droplet-ip>:roreviewapi-backup.tar.gz .

    4. Back on the droplet, delete the archive, so that no extra copy of the secrets is left behind:

      rm ~/roreviewapi-backup.tar.gz

    To check what an archive contains, without unpacking it, run tar -tzf roreviewapi-backup.tar.gz.

    Restoring a backup

    On a rebuilt droplet, restore the backup after getting the code, and before starting the service.

    1. On your own computer, upload the archive to your home directory on the droplet:

      scp roreviewapi-backup.tar.gz <user>@<droplet-ip>:

    2. On the droplet, unpack it, which puts the files back in /srv/roreviewapi/data/ and /home/shared/roreviewapi/.env, then delete the archive:

      sudo tar -xzf ~/roreviewapi-backup.tar.gz -C /
rm ~/roreviewapi-backup.tar.gz

      Unpacking with sudo keeps the original owners and permissions, including the restricted permissions of .env and of the data directory.

    3. If the service is already running, restart it so that it picks up the restored files.

    Updating the operating system

    Update the droplet’s operating system every 2 years. Ubuntu publishes a new long-term support (LTS) release every 2 years, and older releases eventually stop receiving security fixes. Check the current release with:

    lsb_release -a
    1. Download a backup of the data directory and .env first, because rebuilding erases the whole disk.
    2. Use the rebuild feature in Settings of the droplet.
    3. Set the droplet up again by following Starting from scratch, and restore the backup.

    Recreating the certificate

    Create a new certificate when the current one is about to expire, when the key is lost, or when it may have been exposed. Nothing renews the certificate automatically, so check its expiry date with the openssl x509 command in TLS certificate. The current certificate expires on 16 October 2041.

    1. Create a new certificate and install it on the droplet, following steps 1 and 2 of TLS certificate. Replace the key in 1Password with the new one.

    2. Restart nginx so that it loads the new files, and check that the site responds:

      docker compose restart nginx
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://reviewbot.ropensci.org/mean

    3. Revoke the old certificate in SSL/TLS → Origin Server, so that the old key can no longer be used.

    Cloudflare’s Origin CA documentation describes creating, installing and revoking origin certificates in more detail.

    Troubleshooting

    Cloudflare reports problems with the droplet as status codes:

    Status Likely cause
    521 Nothing answers on port 443: nginx or the whole stack is down, or nginx cannot find the certificate files and exits on start
    522 The droplet is unreachable, for example a firewall blocks port 443
    526 The certificate is invalid, expired, or does not match the hostname
    502 nginx is up but plumber is not

    For 521 or 502, check the containers and their logs on the droplet:

    docker compose ps
docker compose logs --tail=50 nginx
docker compose logs --tail=50 plumber
sudo ls /etc/ssl/cloudflare/

    For 522, there are two independent firewalls to check.

    Droplet firewall (ufw):

    sudo ufw status

    If ufw is active and port 443 is not listed, open it:

    sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp

    Digital Ocean cloud firewall: in the Digital Ocean console under Networking → Firewalls, confirm there is an inbound rule allowing TCP port 443. The cloud firewall sits in front of the droplet and blocks traffic before it reaches ufw, so both layers must allow it.

    Optionally, Authenticated Origin Pulls make nginx accept only connections that come through Cloudflare.

    Transferring maintenance

    Maintenance falls into two parts with very different transfer costs:

    • Operations (deploying, debugging, restarting): needs access only. Nothing in .env changes.
    • Credentials tied to an individual: the Gmail authorization, and the GitHub and AirTable tokens, belong to whoever created them. These must be re-created by the new maintainer if the outgoing person’s accounts will be closed.

    Operations only

    When the new person only deploys and debugs, and the existing authorizing account stays active:

    1. Add their SSH key and sudo access on the droplet.
    2. Add them to the roreviewapi GitHub repository.
    3. Add them to the ro-auto-email Google Cloud project’s IAM.
    4. Hand over this document and the contents of .env securely, for example via a password manager rather than email or chat.

    Transferring credentials

    This is required if the outgoing maintainer’s accounts will become unusable, for example on leaving the organization. The values in .env that are tied to a person are:

    Variable Tied to Action on transfer
    GITHUB_PAT GitHub account that created it Replace with a token created by the new maintainer
    AIRTABLE_API_KEY AirTable account that created it Replace with a token created by the new maintainer (see AirTable for the required scope)
    GMAIL_AUTH_EMAIL, GMAIL_TOKEN_CACHE Google account that authorized gmailr Replace, following the Gmail transfer steps in the editor search vignette
    GMAIL_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET, GMAIL_SENDER Google Cloud project and the reviewbot@ropensci.org alias Unchanged if the same Cloud project and alias are kept
    AIRTABLE_BASE_ID, ROREVIEWAPI_BASE_URL, PKGCHECK_TOKEN Not tied to a person Unchanged unless the base, URL or pkgcheck service changes

    The steps are then:

    1. The new maintainer creates their own GitHub and AirTable personal access tokens, and completes the Gmail steps in the editor search vignette.

    2. Update .env on the droplet with the new values.

    3. Restart the service so that the container picks up the new .env and credentials.

    4. Verify that the editor search workflow still sends and receives emails (see the editor search vignette).

    5. Once the new setup works, the outgoing maintainer should revoke their old GitHub and AirTable tokens, and the old Google grant.

    Other items to update

    • Cron job. If the cron job was set up under the outgoing maintainer’s account, move it to root’s crontab (see Cron job), or recreate it under the new account.
    • Git identity. The git config lines in the Dockerfile hold the user.name and user.email used for commits made inside the container.
    • Uptime alert. Whoever receives the uptime alert should be updated.
    • 1Password. The new maintainer needs access to the certificate’s private key.
